title: Cervix & preterm risk
intro: Doctors may say the cervix (the neck of the womb) opened too early. That can be true, but it's often a diagnosis made by ruling other causes out, so the hospital records matter. There's a clear, evidence-based plan for next time, and most women in this position go on to have a baby.

sections.title: What cervical insufficiency is
points: The cervix is the neck of the womb. In a normal pregnancy it stays closed and firm until near the end.
Cervical insufficiency means the cervix shortens and opens too early. This often happens with no pain at all.
You'll hear other names for it: 'incompetent cervix', 'weak cervix', or 'preterm cervical shortening'. They're just labels. None of them means anyone failed.

Known causes include being born with it (a differently shaped womb, or a collagen condition such as Ehlers-Danlos), past cervix surgery (LLETZ or cone biopsy after an abnormal smear), or injury in a previous labour. Many women have no known risk factor.
No test before pregnancy can reliably predict it. A scan or MRI before pregnancy can find a differently shaped womb, though, and that can be a cause.

sections.title: How it's diagnosed (and why to be a bit skeptical)
points: There's no single test for it. It's usually diagnosed after a late miscarriage or premature birth, once other causes have been ruled out.
Mayo Clinic describes the classic picture as the cervix widening without pain (dilation) and the baby being born in the second trimester.
Mayo Clinic calls it 'a hard problem to diagnose', especially in a first pregnancy.
What happened first matters a lot. If contractions, waters breaking, bleeding or fever came before the cervix opened, infection or the placenta may be the real story.
In a future pregnancy, doctors measure the cervix with an internal (transvaginal) scan. A cervix shorter than 25 mm is linked to a higher chance of early birth.

sections.title: Other causes of a mid-pregnancy loss
points: Tommy's says many second-trimester losses are caused by infection. It can reach the baby or the fluid around the baby. When the membranes and fluid are infected, doctors call it chorioamnionitis.
Bacterial vaginosis (BV, an imbalance of vaginal bacteria that often causes no symptoms) raises the risk of a late miscarriage.
Other possible causes are placenta problems, clotting conditions (antiphospholipid syndrome or thrombophilia), and chromosome problems in the baby.
Hospitals can check the placenta and cord under a microscope (histology). They can also run infection tests, blood tests for clotting, thyroid and diabetes, and genetic tests.

In a UK study of over 1,000 post-mortems, the cause was found by looking at the placenta, the clinical notes and the baby's examination. Even so, a clear cause was found for only about 4 in 10 babies.
Results usually take 6 to 12 weeks, sometimes longer. If no full post-mortem was done, you can still ask for the placenta to be examined.

sections.title: What 'higher risk' really means
points: A big Scottish study followed 65,592 women. Those who lost a pregnancy in the second trimester had a 4.3% chance of a spontaneous premature birth next time, compared with 1.5% for other women.
Put the other way round: about 96 in 100 of those women did not have a spontaneous premature birth in their next pregnancy.
In the same study, the chance of another second-trimester loss was 3.7% (against 1.1%). Pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure in pregnancy) was about twice as likely (23.4% against 11.7%).
These are averages for losses up to 24 weeks. The researchers say the evidence is limited. Your own risk depends on the cause, which is another reason to chase the test results.

Treatment helps. A Cochrane review (a gold-standard summary of trials) found that a cervical stitch lowers the chance of early birth in high-risk women. Babies were also less likely to die in their first week.

sections.title: What's done next time
points: If you've had a loss after 16 weeks or a birth before 34 weeks, you should be referred to a specialist early in the next pregnancy.

Option 1 is a planned 'history-indicated' stitch (cerclage), put in around 11 to 14 weeks. UK guidance usually saves this for women with 3 or more losses or early births. Mayo Clinic says it can be used after past cervical insufficiency, so ask which applies to you.
Option 2 is regular internal scans of cervix length between about 16 and 24 weeks. Mayo Clinic describes these as every two weeks.

If the cervix measures 25 mm or less, NICE (the UK guideline body) says to offer a choice: a stitch, or vaginal progesterone (a daily hormone pessary from 16 to 24 weeks until at least 34 weeks). Neither has been shown to beat the other.

If a vaginal stitch has failed before, an abdominal stitch (transabdominal cerclage) is placed higher up, ideally before pregnancy. In a UK trial, 8% of women with one gave birth before 32 weeks, against 33% with a standard vaginal stitch. It stays in, so the baby is born by C-section.
A vaginal stitch usually comes out at 36 to 37 weeks. An emergency stitch, done after the cervix has already opened, is riskier and less likely to work. That's why a plan in early pregnancy matters.

sections.title: Before trying again
points: There's no fixed waiting time. Tommy's suggests giving your body time to recover and waiting for test results so you go in with as much information as possible.
You can get pregnant as early as 3 weeks after giving birth, even before your periods come back. Plan contraception until you're both ready.
Start folic acid before you get pregnant, ideally 3 months before. Vitamin D and not smoking help too.

See a specialist before the next pregnancy. That could be a maternal-fetal medicine (MFM) subspecialist, an obstetrician trained in high-risk pregnancy. An abdominal stitch, if it's ever needed, is best done before pregnancy.
It's common for one partner to feel ready before the other. Talk it through honestly, and get counselling if you need it.

do: Ask the hospital for copies of everything: scan reports, delivery and labour notes, blood and swab results, the placenta histology report, and any post-mortem or genetic results.
While it's fresh, write down your own timeline: when symptoms started, whether there was pain or contractions, when the waters broke, and any bleeding, fever or unusual discharge.
Book the results appointment (usually 6 to 12 weeks after the loss), go together, and take the question list below.
Start folic acid now if a next pregnancy is likely within the next few months.

Before trying again, ask your gynae to refer you to a maternal-fetal medicine subspecialist. Ask your medical aid what it covers for cerclage, progesterone and serial scans, and whether you need pre-authorisation.

Get support for the grief, not just the medicine. The Compassionate Friends in Highlands North runs a pregnancy and infant loss group (011 440 6322, WhatsApp 078 147 2705, tcfsa@mweb.co.za). For a crisis, SADAG's 24-hour line is 0800 567 567.
ask: What exactly makes you think this was the cervix? Did it open without pain, or were there contractions, waters breaking, bleeding or fever first?
Was the placenta sent for histology? Did it show signs of infection (chorioamnionitis) or a placenta problem?
Which infection tests were done, for example swabs for BV? What did they show?
Were tests done for clotting conditions such as antiphospholipid syndrome?
Was a post-mortem or genetic test done or offered? Is it too late to ask for one?
Should I have a scan of my womb's shape before we try again?
Next time, do you recommend a planned stitch at 12 to 14 weeks, or cervix-length scans from 16 weeks? Why that one for me?
Would you add vaginal progesterone? When would I start it, and when would I stop?
If a vaginal stitch doesn't work, would an abdominal stitch be an option? Who does it in Gauteng, and should it be done before pregnancy?
How long do you suggest we wait, and should we see a maternal-fetal medicine specialist first?
Given my history, should my blood pressure be watched more closely next time for pre-eclampsia?
watch_out: Bed rest: a Cochrane review found no evidence that it prevents premature birth, and it carries its own harms. The RCOG says bed rest isn't routinely recommended after a stitch.

Cervical pessary (a silicone ring placed around the cervix): the evidence is mixed. One early trial looked good, but Mayo Clinic says more research is needed, and it isn't part of the NICE recommendations.
A stitch isn't for everyone. It isn't advised with twins, an active infection, bleeding, contractions, or waters that have already broken.
Waiting for symptoms is risky. The cervix can open with no pain, and an emergency stitch works less well than a planned one, so get a plan in early pregnancy.
Warning signs in a future pregnancy: pelvic pressure, a new backache, mild cramps, a change in discharge (especially smelly or green), bleeding, or fluid leaking. Call the maternity unit, don't wait.
Be wary of supplements or 'cervix-strengthening' products sold online. None of the guidelines we checked recommends any.
This was not your fault. Tommy's and Miscarriage UK both say a loss like this is very unlikely to be caused by anything you did or didn't do.

resources.title: Transabdominal vs transvaginal cerclage: a systematic review and meta-analysis
resources.source: Bobotis et al. — American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology
resources.access: Paywalled. Free summary at contemporaryobgyn.net, or email the authors for a copy.
resources.why: The newest pooled look at whether a stitch placed higher up, through the tummy, works better than the usual vaginal stitch.
takeaways: Combined 12 studies with about 1,110 women.
The abdominal stitch was linked to fewer baby deaths around birth (about 64% lower) and less preterm birth (about half).
The benefit looked biggest after a failed vaginal stitch.
The evidence is rated low quality because most studies weren't randomised. A question for the specialist, not a verdict.

resources.title: Transabdominal vs transvaginal cerclage for cervical insufficiency (Mass General Brigham cohort)
resources.source: Messinger et al. — American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology
resources.access: Free summary (hospital press release). Full paper paywalled: doi 10.1016/j.ajog.2025.06.049
resources.why: A large US hospital's real-world results for women with a history of cervical insufficiency.
takeaways: 188 women: 87 had an abdominal stitch, 101 a vaginal one.
The abdominal stitch was linked to about 70% lower risk of birth before 34 weeks.
It's one hospital's records, not a randomised trial.

resources.title: Pre-conceptional laparoscopic cerclage for prevention of preterm birth: a systematic review
resources.source: Facts, Views and Vision in ObGyn
resources.why: Results for a keyhole abdominal stitch placed before getting pregnant, an option some couples choose after a loss like ours.
takeaways: 10 studies, over 1,000 women at high risk.
About 92% of pregnancies ended in a live birth.
About 70% reached full term (37 weeks or later).
No comparison group, so it shows what's possible, not that it beats other options.

resources.title: Cervical Pessary for Prevention of Preterm Birth in Individuals With a Short Cervix: the TOPS trial
resources.why: Why a cervical pessary (a ring around the cervix) is not a good substitute for a stitch.
takeaways: 544 women with a short cervix were randomised to a pessary or usual care.
Preterm birth was the same in both groups, about 45%.
Baby deaths were higher with the pessary (13% vs 7%), so the trial was stopped early.
If a pessary is offered instead of a stitch, ask why.

resources.title: Healing from the Trauma of Pregnancy Loss: Reclaiming Your Reproductive Story
resources.access: Buy (Kindle or import, price not checked)
resources.why: A psychologist who specialises in pregnancy loss explains why it can feel like trauma, and how parents move forward.
takeaways: Published December 2025.
Treats pregnancy loss as a real trauma, not 'just' sadness.
Uses the idea of your 'reproductive story', the hopes you had, to help you rebuild.

resources.title: Hope and Healing After Stillbirth and New Baby Loss (new edition)
resources.source: Kevin Gournay & Brenda Ashcroft — Sheldon Press (Hachette)
resources.access: Buy (Kindle or import, price not checked)
resources.why: Grief after a stillbirth or a baby who dies soon after birth, and the strain it can put on a couple.
takeaways: Updated edition, September 2024.
Covers grief after stillbirth and early baby loss.
Also covers the strain on the relationship that often follows.

resources.title: To Tend and to Hold: Honoring Our Bodies, Our Needs, and Our Grief Through Pregnancy and Infant Loss
resources.access: Buy (Kindle or import, price not checked)
resources.why: For Mishka's body as well as her heart: the physical recovery after a loss that nobody talks about.
takeaways: Covers postpartum care when there's no baby to take home.
Gentle and practical.
Good for both of you to read, so you both understand the physical side.

resources.title: Your Baby Will Find You: A Story about Grief, Loss, and Healing
resources.source: Madeleine Garner, illustrated by Giorgia Lupi — BenBella
resources.access: Buy (Kindle or import, price not checked)
resources.why: A short illustrated book for grown-ups after losing a pregnancy. Something to read together when longer books are too much.
takeaways: Published May 2025.
Mostly pictures, very few words.
Comforting rather than informational.

resources.title: Dads Hurt Too: A Father's Memoir
resources.why: One of the few books written for the father's grief, and how to support your partner while carrying your own.
takeaways: Short, 86 pages, written for the first weeks.
Christian in tone.
Written after miscarriage, but the father's side applies to any baby loss.

resources.title: Cervical stitch (patient information)
resources.source: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG)
resources.why: Updated April 2026. The clearest guide to who gets a stitch, the types, the risks, and what to watch for.
takeaways: RCOG recommends early specialist referral after a loss beyond 16 weeks, birth before 34 weeks or previous early waters breaking.
A stitch supports the cervix but cannot prevent every late loss or preterm birth.
The leaflet describes usual placement between 12 and 24 weeks and removal at 36 to 37 weeks.
Infection, bleeding, contractions or already broken waters can make a stitch unsuitable.
An abdominal stitch may be considered when a vaginal stitch failed or cannot be inserted and requires caesarean birth while present.
Emergency stitches carry more risk and are less likely to succeed than planned stitches.

resources.title: Weak cervix (cervical incompetence): symptoms, causes and treatment
resources.why: A warm, plain overview of diagnosis, scans, progesterone and the different stitches, written without blame.
takeaways: The cervix can shorten and open without pain, so absence of contractions does not exclude a problem.
Possible symptoms include pelvic pressure, bleeding and unusual discharge.
Risk factors include cervical surgery or injury, some uterine differences and conditions affecting collagen [supporting tissue protein].
Tommy's recommends early specialist planning after a late miscarriage or birth before 34 weeks.
The page describes cervical scans usually between 16 and 24 weeks and increased risk below 25 mm.
The page acknowledges that terms such as incompetent cervix can feel blaming and that this is a medical condition.

resources.title: Incompetent cervix: diagnosis and treatment
resources.why: Explains how it's diagnosed and the scan-every-two-weeks approach, and is honest about what's uncertain.
takeaways: Diagnosis depends on pregnancy history and findings such as painless cervical opening, ultrasound measurements and examination.
Mayo says there is no reliable test before pregnancy that predicts cervical insufficiency.
For relevant high-risk histories, the page describes scans every two weeks from 16 through 24 weeks.
Preventive cerclage may be placed before 14 weeks when the previous history supports it.
The page describes vaginal progesterone for a short cervix without previous preterm birth, while a vaginal support pessary needs more evidence.

The supplied URL did not resolve; the verified diagnosis-and-treatment page uses [drc-20373842](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/incompetent-cervix/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20373842?p=1).

resources.title: Preterm labour and birth (NG25): recommendations
resources.why: The actual guideline doctors follow. Section 1.2 covers progesterone and the stitch, if you want to check the source yourselves.
takeaways: NICE offers a choice of preventive vaginal progesterone or cerclage when both qualifying pregnancy history and cervical length 25 mm or less are present.
The qualifying history includes spontaneous birth up to 34 weeks or loss from 16 weeks onward.
NICE also allows consideration of progesterone with either history or short cervix alone, a difference from current ACOG recurrent-birth guidance.
When prescribed under this guideline, progesterone starts between 16 and 24 weeks and continues to at least 34 weeks.
Emergency cerclage can be considered from 16 weeks through 27 weeks and 6 days with an open cervix and exposed but unruptured membranes.
Infection, active bleeding or contractions rule out emergency cerclage under these recommendations.

resources.title: Second trimester loss: tests, post-mortem and follow-up
resources.why: Lists the tests to ask about, including placenta histology, and how to get the most from the follow-up appointment.
takeaways: The original link redirects to Miscarriage UK's broader second-trimester-loss page.
Possible causes include chromosome differences, fetal structural problems, placental disease, uterine or cervical problems and infection.
Chromosome testing using fetal or placental tissue can sometimes identify a cause and inform future risk.
The page describes antiphospholipid syndrome [an immune-related clotting disorder] as one possible placental cause.
When cervical weakness is suspected, it describes discussing a stitch in a future pregnancy, usually around 13 or 14 weeks.
Its miscarriage and registration discussion follows UK definitions, so do not apply its legal wording directly to a 25-week loss in South Africa.

resources.title: Second trimester pregnancy and baby loss linked to higher risks in future pregnancies
resources.why: Honest, real-world recurrence numbers from 65,000+ women, plus a reminder that most go on without complications.
takeaways: The February 2026 news release describes a study of 65,592 women with first and second pregnancies recorded in Aberdeen between 1950 and 2017.
It reports spontaneous preterm birth in the next pregnancy in 4.3% after an initial second-trimester loss versus 1.5% in the comparison group.
Repeat second-trimester loss occurred in 3.7% versus 1.1%, so higher relative risk still meant a minority had another loss.
The release also reports increased early miscarriage and pre-eclampsia and calls for clearer follow-up pathways.
The linked study defined the original loss as before 24 weeks and was observational, so it does not provide a personalised recurrence estimate after a 25-week loss.
Its finding of no detected increase in spontaneous preterm birth after termination for medical reasons was limited by a small sample.

resources.title: Can inserting a cervical stitch prevent early births?
resources.why: A plain-language summary of 15 trials: what the stitch can and can't do.
takeaways: This 2017 Cochrane update included fifteen trials involving 3,490 women with singleton pregnancies.
It compared stitches with no stitch or alternative treatment in women considered at risk from their history, scans or examination.
Cerclage reduced preterm birth compared with no cerclage in the reviewed evidence.
For death around birth, the pooled relative risk was 0.82 with a 95% confidence interval from 0.65 to 1.04, leaving uncertainty about a mortality benefit.
The review had too little direct comparison evidence to settle whether cerclage was better than progesterone.
The supplied summary link was unavailable during checking; the same review is readable in [PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6481522).

resources.title: MAVRIC trial: abdominal vs vaginal cerclage (abstract)
resources.source: American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology, 2020 (Shennan et al.)
resources.why: The key trial showing an abdominal stitch works better when a vaginal stitch has failed.
takeaways: MAVRIC studied women whose previous vaginal stitch had failed, not everyone after a first late loss.
The analysis included 111 pregnancies: 39 abdominal stitches, 39 high vaginal stitches and 33 low vaginal stitches.
Birth before 32 weeks occurred in 8% with an abdominal stitch versus 33% with a low vaginal stitch.
The high vaginal group had a 38% rate and did not improve on the low vaginal group.
An exploratory analysis found fetal loss in 3% with an abdominal stitch versus 21% with a low vaginal stitch.
The supplied abstract host was unavailable; figures were checked against the [published PubMed abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31585096/).

resources.title: Trying for another baby after stillbirth or neonatal death
resources.why: Gentle, practical help with timing, waiting for results, and being ready as a couple.
takeaways: Whether and when to try again is a personal decision without one timetable that fits every family.
Partners may feel ready at different times, and the page encourages honest conversation and support.
Physical recovery and mental readiness are separate considerations.
Waiting for investigation results can help inform a future pregnancy plan.
Age, general health and fertility treatment can also influence timing discussions.
Tommy's describes specialist pregnancy-after-loss support through UK Rainbow Clinics; this is a service model rather than a Johannesburg referral route.

resources.title: Finding the reasons for premature birth
resources.why: A 2-minute look at the research behind preterm birth clinics.
takeaways: Tommy's published this short educational animation on 8 September 2019.
Its verified description gives a historical UK figure of around 60,000 premature births each year.
It explains that many early births remain unexplained and that clinicians do not fully understand every cause.
The animation introduces Tommy's research on predicting and preventing premature birth.
The verified description and charity campaign page support these points, but the video transcript was unavailable, so no specific treatment claims are attributed to the footage.

resources.title: Abdominal cerclage: a solution to second trimester pregnancy loss
resources.why: A surgeon and a patient explain the abdominal stitch, the option if a vaginal stitch fails.
takeaways: Northwell Health published this patient-story video on 15 July 2025.
Its description features Dr Michael Nimaroff and a patient who grew her family after abdominal cerclage.
The provider presents the operation as an option when other approaches have failed.
It is a hospital-produced individual success story, so it supplies neither a comparison group nor a personal success probability.
Only the verified video description was accessible, so its selection criteria, complication rates and spoken clinical details could not be independently checked here.

resources.title: Bearing the Unbearable: Love, Loss, and the Heartbreaking Path of Grief
resources.why: 52 short chapters by a bereaved mother and grief researcher. Easy to read one at a time, together.
takeaways: The publisher describes grief as nonlinear and often lasting longer than other people expect.
The book contains 52 short, standalone chapters that can be read in small amounts or in a support group.
Joanne Cacciatore draws on bereavement work and her own daughter Cheyenne's death in 1994.
The stated approach is to process and honour grief through stories and connection.
The linked edition was published in June 2017 and is listed as 248 pages.
These points are verified from the publisher's description; the page does not establish a clinical treatment effect or a timetable for recovery.

resources.title: The Compassionate Friends: pregnancy and infant loss support group (Highlands North, Johannesburg)
resources.source: Rosebank Killarney Gazette / The Compassionate Friends
resources.why: A free, peer-led group for miscarriage, stillbirth and baby loss, which also helps couples who grieve differently. Call 011 440 6322 or WhatsApp 078 147 2705.
takeaways: The February 2025 article announced a Highlands North group for miscarriage, stillbirth and death of a baby under two.
It described support for parents, grandparents and siblings.
The reporting recognises sadness, isolation, guilt and anger as possible grief responses.
It highlights that partners can grieve differently and may need help communicating.
The published contact numbers were WhatsApp 078 147 2705 and telephone 011 440 6322.
Its first-session date of 8 March 2025 is historical, so use the organisation's current contact details to confirm the next meeting.

resources.title: Maternal and Fetal Medicine Unit, Steve Biko Academic Hospital (Pretoria)
resources.why: A public high-risk pregnancy unit with a recurrent pregnancy loss clinic. Ask for a referral if you're going the state route.
takeaways: The University of Pretoria unit provides specialist care for high-risk pregnancies and fetal wellbeing.
It runs services at both Steve Biko Academic Hospital and Kalafong Provincial Tertiary Hospital.
The page lists a recurrent-pregnancy-loss clinic on Tuesdays at Steve Biko and Thursdays at Kalafong.
Steve Biko also lists general high-risk, fetal and specialised maternal clinics.
The listed Steve Biko contacts include 012 354 2849, fetal clinic 012 354 3717 and maternal clinic 012 354 3716.
Confirm referral eligibility, clinic days and current availability before travelling from Edenvale; the page does not promise direct booking or cerclage access.

resources.title: Updated progestogen guidance for preventing recurrent preterm birth
resources.source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
resources.why: Explains the evidence change behind conflicting progesterone advice.
takeaways: Vaginal progesterone can be considered after a previous preterm birth when the current singleton pregnancy also has a shortened cervix.
ACOG advises against offering it for recurrent preterm-birth prevention when the cervix is not shortened.
Intramuscular 17-OHPC [a synthetic hormone injection] is no longer recommended for recurrent preterm-birth prevention.
ACOG recommends repeated transvaginal cervical-length assessment after a previous spontaneous preterm birth.
The plan should reflect the pregnancy history, cervical measurements and previous treatment response.

resources.title: SMFM Consult 65: Transabdominal cerclage
resources.source: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine; endorsed by ACOG and AAGL
resources.why: Defines when abdominal surgery is justified and what it commits a family to.
takeaways: Offer abdominal cerclage after a history-based or scan-based vaginal stitch followed by spontaneous singleton delivery before 28 weeks.
A maternal-fetal medicine consultation is recommended for potential candidates.
Open surgery and laparoscopy [keyhole surgery] are both acceptable when matched to expertise and circumstances.
Placement before pregnancy or in the first trimester has similar fetal outcomes; selected later presentations can be considered before 22 weeks.
Routine cervical-length screening is not recommended while an abdominal stitch is in place.
The guidance suggests caesarean delivery between 37 and 39 weeks with the stitch in place.

resources.title: SMFM Consult 70: Short cervix without previous spontaneous preterm birth
resources.why: Shows why treatment advice for a first short cervix differs from advice after an early birth.
takeaways: This document's main population has no previous spontaneous preterm birth, an important limit if you've already had an early birth or loss.
Use a transvaginal measurement of 25 mm or less to identify a short cervix in this population.
Recommend vaginal progesterone for an asymptomatic singleton pregnancy with cervical length 20 mm or less before 24 weeks.
Consider progesterone at 21 to 25 mm through shared decision-making.
For a closed cervix measuring 10 to 25 mm without prior preterm birth, routine cerclage is not recommended.
A cervical pessary [support device] is not recommended for singleton short-cervix prevention.

resources.title: FIGO good practice recommendations on cervical cerclage
resources.source: FIGO; Shennan, Story, Jacobsson and Grobman
resources.why: A short international statement separating the main stitch indications.
takeaways: FIGO recommends a history-based stitch after three or more previous preterm deliveries or mid-trimester losses.
It recommends a scan-based stitch for cervical length under 25 mm with one or more previous spontaneous early births or mid-trimester losses.
For women with three or more previous events in a cited trial subgroup, birth before 33 weeks occurred in 15% with cerclage versus 32% without it.
Rescue cerclage with exposed membranes needs individual assessment because infection can threaten mother and baby.
A stitch is generally removed at 36 to 37 weeks when vaginal birth is planned.

resources.title: Preterm labour with intact membranes, version 2
resources.source: SASOG BetterObs; Mediclinic clinical team and BetterObs reviewers
resources.why: Shows the South African hospital response when early labour is suspected.
takeaways: The protocol lists previous second-trimester loss, preterm birth and cervical procedures as risk factors.
Assessment includes leaking fluid, contractions, pressure, backache, urinary symptoms, discharge and bleeding.
The team should verify gestational age and review the antenatal records and blood results.
Initial examination includes maternal vital signs, urine testing and assessment of uterine activity.
The document was released on 20 January 2023 after BetterObs revision in 2022.
Its authors explicitly require clinical judgement and individualised care rather than using the protocol alone.

resources.title: National Integrated Maternal and Perinatal Care Guidelines for South Africa
resources.source: South African National Department of Health
resources.why: The key local reference for referral and prevention planning in the public system.
takeaways: After stillbirth or pregnancy-related neonatal death, hospital assessment should follow the first booking visit.
Cerclage belongs at a specialist referral centre for selected singleton pregnancies.
Indications include three previous preterm births or second-trimester losses, or a short cervix plus one qualifying event.
The short-cervix threshold is 25 mm or less before 24 weeks.
The section lists vaginal progesterone 200 mg daily until 34 weeks as an alternative with a short cervix, for clinician assessment.
Mental-health support and respectful care are part of management after a poor pregnancy outcome.

resources.title: Caesarean vs vaginal birth: A mother's choice, not her doctor's
resources.why: Investigates SA maternity decisions, litigation fears and patient choice.
takeaways: The article reports that 68% of scheme-funded births in 2015 were caesareans, a historical figure rather than a current national rate.
CMS said those data did not separate scheme-funded births in private and public hospitals.
Interviewed clinicians describe litigation risk and professional insurance costs as pressures on birth decisions.
The reporting also describes scheduling preferences among some parents.
The article stresses disclosure of both vaginal-birth and caesarean risks so women can make informed choices.
It is about birth mode, so it does not establish whether a cerclage is needed after a particular loss.

resources.title: It's a Stick-Up. Your Money or Your Health!
resources.why: An accessible, explicitly critical explanation of the private-care inquiry.
takeaways: This commentary explains the inquiry's provisional 2018 findings, rather than reporting current prices.
It says the inquiry examined more than 43 million patient records and 11 million admissions.
It reports average spending per member rising 9.2% annually during 2010 to 2014.
Even after adjustments, the inquiry found an unexplained real increase above 2% annually.
The article explains information asymmetry [providers knowing more than patients] as a barrier to judging value.
It separates nonprofit medical schemes from commercial administrators and discusses concentrated hospital ownership.

resources.title: PMB questions and answers
resources.why: Bookmark the regulator's explanation before requesting funding approval.
takeaways: Schemes can require pre-authorisation and participation in a benefit-management programme.
Voluntary use of a non-DSP [a provider outside the designated network] can result in a permitted co-payment.
Involuntary non-DSP use has protections, including relevant emergencies and lack of reasonable access to a DSP.
Medicine formularies [approved lists] can affect the price difference a member pays for a preferred brand.
These rules explain PMB administration but do not promise that every progesterone prescription qualifies.

resources.title: The complaints procedure
resources.why: A concrete route for disputing a scheme's funding decision.
takeaways: First use the scheme's internal complaints and dispute process.
CMS asks for the facts, requested remedy and proof of prior escalation.
Clinical disputes need the relevant clinical reports; unpaid-claim disputes need account statements.
Someone submitting a complaint on the member's behalf needs signed consent.
The page gives an ordinary resolution target of 120 calendar days after the scheme response and complete documents, while clinically urgent complaints are handled urgently.
CMS cannot award compensation for pain and suffering.

resources.title: The Discovery Day Surgery Network
resources.why: Contains a direct SA funding reference to cerclage and stitch removal.
takeaways: The procedure list explicitly includes uterine cervix cerclage and removal of a cerclage suture.
It describes network facilities for specified same-day procedures on several plan series.
Executive-plan members can use any approved facility according to this page.
Planned admissions require pre-authorisation.
Cover remains subject to the chosen plan, so listing a procedure is not an individual payment guarantee.
Confirm the current facility rule for the actual operation, especially if an abdominal procedure or overnight admission is proposed.

resources.title: Maternity Benefit
resources.why: A useful worked example of routine allowances, activation and reimbursement limits.
takeaways: The My Pregnancy or My Baby programme must be activated to access the described maternity benefits.
The page lists up to eight or twelve antenatal consultations depending on the plan.
Routine ultrasound cover is up to two 2D scans or one nuchal translucency test [an early screening scan].
Services are paid at the Discovery Health Rate, which is the scheme's reimbursement rate.
The described maternity benefit does not use day-to-day benefits, while childbirth is funded through the Hospital Benefit.
The page includes two postnatal mental-health consultations, but does not establish eligibility after every type of loss.

resources.title: Maternal Fetal Medicine Division
resources.why: Identifies relevant Johannesburg academic services for a referral request.
takeaways: The division lists specialised referral clinics rather than a general pregnancy-information service.
Poor Obstetrics History [care after serious previous pregnancy problems] is a named clinic.
Perinatal Mental Health [mental health around pregnancy and birth] is another named clinic.
The list also includes medical high-risk and fetal-medicine clinics.
The page does not specify a cervical-insufficiency booking pathway, so confirm the destination and referral requirements with the care team.

resources.title: Dr Jayshree Jeebodh, maternal-fetal specialist, Park Lane
resources.why: A verifiable private Johannesburg specialist contact for assessing service fit.
takeaways: The practice identifies Dr Jeebodh as a maternal-fetal medicine subspecialist since 2007.
The listed address is Netcare Park Lane Hospital, Parklane Medical Centre, 15 on Junction, Parktown.
The listed telephone number is 010 447 3725.
Services include high-risk counselling, first-trimester assessment, anatomy scans and growth scans.
The page says an internal scan may be needed to assess the cervix.
It does not publish cerclage outcomes, fees or a dedicated prevention-clinic schedule, so confirm those before booking.

resources.title: Pregnancy and Infant Loss Support Group: primary-source 2026 listing
resources.why: Updates the older newspaper resource with the organisation's own local listing.
takeaways: The group supports parents after miscarriage, stillbirth or death in early infancy.
The listed venue is 122 Athol Street, Highlands North, Johannesburg.
This event ran on 8 August 2026 from 14:00 to 16:00, so it is evidence of a recent service rather than a future appointment.
The organisation lists 011 440 6322 and WhatsApp or SMS 078 147 2705 for joining.
The contact email is tcfsa@mweb.co.za; ask for the next date and whether both partners can attend together.

resources.title: Vaginal progesterone for singleton pregnancies with a short cervix: individual-patient meta-analysis
resources.source: Romero and colleagues, American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
resources.why: Provides the main absolute benefit figures behind short-cervix progesterone treatment.
takeaways: The analysis combined individual data from 974 women across five high-quality trials.
Participants had a singleton pregnancy and a mid-pregnancy cervical length of 25 mm or less.
Birth before 33 weeks occurred in approximately 14% with vaginal progesterone versus 22% with placebo.
The pooled relative risk was 0.62, meaning a 38% relative reduction rather than a 38-percentage-point reduction.
The authors estimated that about twelve women would need treatment to prevent one birth before 33 weeks in these trial populations.
Measured developmental outcomes at age two did not differ between treatment and placebo groups.

resources.title: SuPPoRT: comparing cervical cerclage, pessary and vaginal progesterone
resources.why: A direct comparison that helps explain why treatment choices remain contested.
takeaways: The UK trial randomised 386 women with a singleton pregnancy and a cervix under 25 mm.
Entry was between 14 weeks and 23 weeks and 6 days across 19 maternity units.
More than 85% had a previous risk factor, but only 39.1% had a previous spontaneous early birth or mid-trimester loss.
Birth before 37 weeks occurred in 39 of 127 cerclage participants, 38 of 122 pessary participants and 32 of 132 progesterone participants.
Treatments met the trial's 20-percentage-point equivalence margin [the allowed difference], which does not prove identical effects in every subgroup.
Recruitment stopped early during COVID-19 and the trial was underpowered for newborn outcomes; the page links a 2025 correction.

resources.title: The NLRP3 inflammasome and the mechanisms of cervical ripening
resources.why: An advanced biology layer for understanding why cervical change is not purely mechanical.
takeaways: Cervical ripening [softening before birth] involves changes in the tissue's supporting structure.
The review describes collagen and elastin breakdown alongside increased tissue hydration.
Hyaluronic acid [a molecule that holds water] contributes to the changing tissue environment.
Local inflammatory processes are part of the remodelling discussion.
The role of the NLRP3 inflammasome [an immune signalling complex] in cervical tissue remains incompletely understood.
This is a mechanisms review, not evidence that an inflammasome test or targeted drug is established care after a loss.

resources.title: Ask Me His Name: Learning to Live and Laugh Again After the Loss of My Baby
resources.why: A parent's account of life after baby loss, separate from clinical prevention advice.
takeaways: The publisher describes a memoir about Elle Wright's pregnancy, her son Teddy and life after his death.
Teddy was born in May 2016 and died three days later.
The account explores leaving hospital without a baby and navigating an unanticipated form of parenthood.
The English edition is listed as 320 pages and was released on 6 September 2018.
The publisher says a portion of sales supports Tommy's; these points come from the publisher description rather than a full-text review.

resources.title: Cerclage: At Your Cervix! with Dr Andrei Rebarber
resources.source: Healthful Woman; Dr Nathan Fox and Dr Andrei Rebarber
resources.why: A conversational explanation of the surgery's history and the problem of choosing candidates.
takeaways: The episode explains that cerclage has been used since the 1950s, before modern trial standards were common.
The hosts describe the central controversy as deciding who actually needs the operation and when.
They distinguish stitches based on pregnancy history, ultrasound findings and examination findings.
Their page summary describes most vaginal procedures as taking around half an hour or less under anaesthesia.
Their practice generally removes a vaginal stitch at 36 to 37 weeks if earlier labour has not occurred.
This is a US specialist discussion published before the 2023 progesterone changes, so use newer guidelines for current medication decisions.

resources.title: Health Market Inquiry: final findings and recommendations
resources.why: The primary evidence archive behind claims about private healthcare incentives.
takeaways: The inquiry investigated features that prevent, distort or restrict competition in private healthcare.
Its archive links the final report, executive summary and presentation of findings.
The report identifies high and rising spending without credible corresponding evidence of improved outcomes.
It examines hospital concentration, funder behaviour and payment incentives rather than blaming one profession alone.
Its recommendations are proposals for reform, not proof that every proposed reform has since been implemented.
Use the 2019 findings to frame questions about value, while checking present-day prices and scheme rules separately.

resources.title: Gauteng free maternity-care policy after the High Court order
resources.source: SECTION27 and the Centre for Child Law
resources.why: Explains an important Gauteng access ruling from the organisations involved.
takeaways: The statement concerns compliance with an April 2023 Gauteng High Court order on free public healthcare.
The protected groups include pregnant and breastfeeding women and children under six.
The ruling addressed access regardless of nationality and documentation status, including hospital services.
The organisations reported amended policy alongside only partial compliance in October 2023.
An access right does not guarantee an immediate specialist appointment or a chosen private hospital, so referral and service availability still need confirmation.

who_pays: Public maternity care is funded mainly through taxes and provincial health budgets; the National Health Act provides free public health services for pregnant women who are not medical scheme beneficiaries, subject to its conditions. [National Health Act](https://www.health.gov.za/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/nhrec-train_NationalHealthAct.pdf)

In private care, medical schemes pool members' monthly contributions, while families pay costs outside their cover or above applicable reimbursement rates. [How medical schemes work](https://www.discovery.co.za/medical-aid/how-medical-schemes-work)

PMBs [prescribed minimum benefits, the legal minimum cover] protect qualifying diagnosis, treatment and care, but provider rules and lawful waiting periods can affect payment. [CMS PMB Q&A](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/pmb-questions/) [CMS pregnancy waiting-period ruling](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/download/3773/2025/30041/m-v-discovery-health-medical-scheme_june-2025.pdf)

There is no verified universal cerclage price or blanket progesterone funding promise in these sources, so obtain a written decision for the actual diagnosis, procedure, medicine and plan. [CMS conditions](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/resources/pmb/pmb-conditions/)
who_decides: The patient gives informed consent after the clinician explains the diagnosis, alternatives, benefits, risks and costs, with her partner involved as she wishes. [National Health Act, sections 6 and 7](https://www.health.gov.za/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/nhrec-train_NationalHealthAct.pdf)

The obstetrician and MFM specialist [maternal-fetal medicine doctor, a specialist in complicated pregnancies] interpret the previous loss and recommend monitoring or treatment. [RCOG cervical stitch](https://www.rcog.org.uk/for-the-public/browse-our-patient-information/cervical-stitch/)

Public referral teams and hospital capacity influence where specialist care happens, while scheme authorisation teams decide funding under the scheme rules and PMB law. [SA maternity guidelines](https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2024-10/Integrated%20Maternal%20and%20Perinatal%20Care%20Guideline_Final%204%20October%202024%20%20DG%20signed.pdf) [CMS PMB Q&A](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/pmb-questions/)

Funding disputes can go through the scheme's complaints process and then the Council for Medical Schemes, which regulates schemes. [CMS complaints](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/consumer-assistance/complaintsprocedure/)
who_profits: Private hospitals, specialist practices, laboratories and medicine suppliers receive payments for the services or products they provide. [Health Market Inquiry](https://www.compcom.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Final-Findings-and-recommendations-report-Health-Market-Inquiry.pdf)

Medical schemes themselves are nonprofit funds, while a separate commercial administrator can earn fees for managing them. [Discovery's explanation of the distinction](https://www.discovery.co.za/medical-aid/how-medical-schemes-work)

The 2019 Health Market Inquiry found that fee-for-service [payment for each service] and weak information about quality encouraged excess use across private healthcare. [Inquiry findings](https://www.compcom.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Final-Findings-and-recommendations-report-Health-Market-Inquiry.pdf)

That finding supports asking why an intervention is needed, but does not prove that a particular clinician's recommendation is financially motivated. [SAMJ explanation of the inquiry](https://www.scielo.org.za/scielo.php?pid=S0256-95742020000200006&script=sci_arttext)

SA reporting also identifies litigation fears and scheduling pressures in maternity decisions, so financial incentives are only part of the picture. [Bhekisisa maternity investigation](https://bhekisisa.org/article/2016-11-11-00-caesarean-vs-vaginal-birth-a-mothers-choice-not-her-doctors/)
what_it_means_for_us: Arrange a specialist review of the 25-week loss before another pregnancy if possible, because painless cervical opening, labour, infection and waters breaking first can lead to different prevention plans. [Mayo diagnosis and treatment](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/incompetent-cervix/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20373842?p=1)

Ask the specialist to explain whether the next pregnancy needs an early planned stitch or cervical scans with a treatment trigger, and have that plan written down. [RCOG cervical stitch](https://www.rcog.org.uk/for-the-public/browse-our-patient-information/cervical-stitch/)

For public care, ask the local clinic or obstetric team to arrange referral to an appropriate high-risk service; Wits lists poor-obstetric-history and perinatal mental-health clinics. [Wits MFM division](https://www.wits.ac.za/clinicalmed/departments/obstetrics-and-gynaecology/academic-divisions/maternal-fetal-medicine-division/)

For private care, request an itemised quotation in Rands and written scheme approval covering the surgeon, anaesthetist, facility, scans, medicine and stitch removal separately. [Discovery day-surgery rules](https://www.discovery.co.za/medical-aid/day-surgery-network) [CMS PMB Q&A](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/pmb-questions/)

Make grief support part of the care plan, and confirm the next pregnancy-loss group meeting with The Compassionate Friends in Highlands North on 011 440 6322 or WhatsApp 078 147 2705. [Organisation's 2026 listing](https://www.compassionatefriends.co.za/supportgroups/general-grief-support-group-14-june-kdwp7-z8czs-wjn7g)

deep_sections.title: Reconstruct the loss before naming the cause
points: A single mid-pregnancy loss does not by itself establish cervical insufficiency [the cervix opening too early without the usual labour process]. [Mayo diagnosis](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/incompetent-cervix/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20373842?p=1)

Build a timeline from the records showing when pressure, bleeding, contractions, cervical opening and leaking fluid first appeared, because their order helps the specialist assess the mechanism. [SASOG-hosted assessment guidance](https://sasog.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/PRETERM-LABOUR-WITH-INTACT-MEMBRANES-2.0.pdf)

PPROM [waters breaking before labour and before 37 weeks] is a different starting event from painless opening with intact membranes, although these processes can overlap. [NICE NG25](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng25/chapter/recommendations)

Ask for the cervical examination notes, ultrasound reports, infection results, delivery summary and any placental histology [microscope examination of the placenta] to be reviewed together, rather than relying on a discharge label. [Loss investigations](https://www.miscarriageuk.org/types-of-pregnancy-loss/second-trimester-loss-late-miscarriage/)

Cervical tissue changes involve collagen [supporting protein], water content and inflammatory signals, so the biology is more complex than a cervix that simply cannot carry weight. [Cervical remodelling review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11012148/)

A cerclage [a stitch supporting the cervix] does not treat every pathway to preterm birth, so infection, bleeding and contractions change the decision. [UCLH patient guidance](https://www.uclh.nhs.uk/patients-and-visitors/patient-information-pages/cervical-cerclage)

There is no reliable test outside pregnancy that proves how the cervix will behave in a future pregnancy. [Mayo diagnosis](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/incompetent-cervix/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20373842?p=1)

The Aberdeen study defines the previous second-trimester loss as 13 weeks to 23 weeks and 6 days, so its recurrence percentages do not directly describe a previous birth or loss after 24 weeks. [PASTeL-2 paper](https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/1471-0528.70161)

deep_sections.title: Why guidelines can disagree
points: History-indicated, ultrasound-indicated and examination-indicated stitches are three different decisions based on past events, scan findings or an already opening cervix. [FIGO recommendations](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291060/)

FIGO recommends a history-based stitch after three or more preterm births or mid-trimester losses, but also recommends a scan-based stitch after one such event when cervical length is under 25 mm. [FIGO recommendations](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291060/)

Those thresholds do not mean a couple must lose three babies before specialist review or a prevention plan. [RCOG early-referral advice](https://www.rcog.org.uk/for-the-public/browse-our-patient-information/cervical-stitch/)

NICE allows consideration of vaginal progesterone based on prior spontaneous preterm birth or qualifying loss alone, while ACOG advises against offering it for recurrent preterm birth without a shortened cervix. [NICE NG25](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng25/chapter/recommendations) [ACOG advisory](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/practice-advisory/articles/2023/04/updated-guidance-use-of-progestogen-supplementation-for-prevention-of-recurrent-preterm-birth)

South Africa's 2024 national maternity guideline describes progesterone as an alternative to cerclage when a short cervix is confirmed before 24 weeks. [National maternity guideline](https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2024-10/Integrated%20Maternal%20and%20Perinatal%20Care%20Guideline_Final%204%20October%202024%20%20DG%20signed.pdf)

SMFM Consult 70 concerns people without previous spontaneous preterm birth, so its recommendation against routine stitches for a closed short cervix cannot simply be applied to someone with a previous spontaneous 25-week birth. [SMFM Consult 70](https://assets.noviams.com/novi-file-uploads/smfm/Publications_and_Guidelines/Consults/Short_Cervix_FINAL_PDF_AJOG.pdf)

Ask which guideline fits the actual history and why the clinician's recommendation follows or differs from it, because a guideline threshold is a decision aid rather than an individual prognosis. [ACOG collaborative planning](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/practice-advisory/articles/2023/04/updated-guidance-use-of-progestogen-supplementation-for-prevention-of-recurrent-preterm-birth)

Treatment-guiding cervical measurements should use a standard transvaginal scan [an ultrasound probe in the vagina], rather than treating an abdominal estimate as interchangeable. [SMFM Consult 70](https://assets.noviams.com/novi-file-uploads/smfm/Publications_and_Guidelines/Consults/Short_Cervix_FINAL_PDF_AJOG.pdf)

deep_sections.title: Read treatment claims in absolute numbers
points: The 2018 progesterone analysis found birth before 33 weeks in about 14% with treatment versus 22% with placebo among singleton pregnancies with a short cervix. [Individual-patient meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5987201/)

That is about eight fewer early births per 100 treated in the study population, rather than a promise that progesterone prevents every early birth. [Individual-patient meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5987201/)

A confidence interval [the range showing statistical uncertainty] that crosses no difference means a study has not established a clear benefit for that outcome. [Cochrane cerclage review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6481522)

MAVRIC tested abdominal stitches after a previous vaginal stitch had failed, so its strong results support a selected rescue strategy for future pregnancies rather than routine abdominal surgery after any loss. [Published trial abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31585096/)

An abdominal stitch brings surgical risks and usually remains in place, with caesarean birth required while it is present. [SMFM Consult 65](https://publications.smfm.org/publications/471-society-for-maternal-fetal-medicine-consult-series-65/)

SuPPoRT found similar outcomes across three treatments within its chosen equivalence margin [the maximum difference the trial accepted as similar], but was too small to settle uncommon newborn outcomes. [SuPPoRT](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.1004427)

TOPS found no benefit and a mortality concern with a cervical pessary [a silicone support device], in a different population with no prior spontaneous preterm birth. [TOPS](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2807569)

Combining a stitch with progesterone should have an explicit reason, because these sources do not establish that every high-risk patient benefits from both. [SMFM shared-decision recommendation](https://publications.smfm.org/publications/471-society-for-maternal-fetal-medicine-consult-series-65/)

Makena was injectable 17-OHPC [a synthetic progestogen], and its US approval was withdrawn in 2023 after benefit was not confirmed; that decision does not invalidate vaginal progesterone for a short cervix. [FDA decision](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-commissioner-and-chief-scientist-announce-decision-withdraw-approval-makena) [ACOG advisory](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/practice-advisory/articles/2023/04/updated-guidance-use-of-progestogen-supplementation-for-prevention-of-recurrent-preterm-birth)

Routine bed rest has no demonstrated preventive benefit and can harm physical health, income and mental wellbeing. [SMFM activity-restriction guidance](https://cdn.smfm.org.s3.amazonaws.com/attachments/767/627ea438ca531a251adf7dbb7ee50eb9.pdf)

deep_sections.title: Turn medical-aid language into a funding decision
points: A PMB diagnosis must meet its legal descriptor, so an ICD-10 code [a diagnosis billing code] alone does not establish entitlement. [CMS conditions](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/resources/pmb/pmb-conditions/)

A DSP [designated service provider] is the scheme's selected provider for qualifying care, and voluntarily using another provider can trigger a permitted co-payment. [CMS PMB Q&A](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/pmb-questions/)

Ask the specialist's practice to submit the clinical indication and exact procedure codes, then ask the scheme to specify which benefit pays each item. [CMS coding explanation](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/resources/pmb/?trk=public_profile__posts-text)

Ask separately whether the prescribed vaginal progesterone formulation, quantity and duration are covered, including any formulary [approved-medicine list] or exception process. [CMS medicine rules](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/pmb-questions/)

The inclusion of cervical cerclage on Discovery's day-surgery list shows that facility rules can matter even when the procedure is recognised. [Discovery procedure list](https://www.discovery.co.za/medical-aid/day-surgery-network)

An advertised maternity allowance for routine scans does not establish how a medically required series of cervical scans will be funded. [Discovery maternity cover](https://www.discovery.co.za/medical-aid/maternity-benefit)

A hospital package is not necessarily the full bill: one Mediclinic caesarean page lists R34,255 but excludes doctors, radiology, pathology and independent care for the baby, so use it only as an example of exclusions. [Hospital package](https://www.mediclinic.co.za/en/corporate/private-fixed-fees/caesarean-section.html)

For a denial, request the written rule and clinical reason, keep the specialist's motivation and accounts, and use the scheme's complaints process before CMS. [CMS complaint requirements](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/consumer-assistance/complaintsprocedure/)

Joining a scheme while pregnant does not guarantee immediate PMB funding, because lawful waiting periods can apply in some membership histories. [CMS 2025 ruling](https://www.medicalschemes.co.za/download/3773/2025/30041/m-v-discovery-health-medical-scheme_june-2025.pdf)

deep_sections.title: Plan the route before the next emergency
points: Book specialist review early enough to discuss a planned stitch before symptoms or shortening occur. [UCLH timing guidance](https://www.uclh.nhs.uk/patients-and-visitors/patient-information-pages/cervical-cerclage)

For Edenvale, confirm the public referral destination with the local care team rather than assuming that any academic clinic accepts direct walk-ins. [SA referral guidance](https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2024-10/Integrated%20Maternal%20and%20Perinatal%20Care%20Guideline_Final%204%20October%202024%20%20DG%20signed.pdf)

Wits lists a Poor Obstetrics History clinic and a Perinatal Mental Health clinic, which are useful service descriptions when requesting referral. [Wits division](https://www.wits.ac.za/clinicalmed/departments/obstetrics-and-gynaecology/academic-divisions/maternal-fetal-medicine-division/)

In private care, a fetal anatomy scan appointment and an ongoing preterm-birth prevention service may serve different needs, so confirm who will prescribe treatment and act on cervical changes. [Park Lane MFM practice services](https://jeebodh.co.za/)

If another pregnancy develops leaking fluid, bleeding, contractions, fever or concerning pelvic pressure, contact maternity triage promptly rather than waiting for the next scheduled scan. [RCOG warning signs](https://www.rcog.org.uk/for-the-public/browse-our-patient-information/cervical-stitch/)

If very early birth threatens, ask which hospital can provide the required neonatal care and whether transfer before birth is possible. [SASOG-hosted preterm-labour protocol](https://sasog.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/PRETERM-LABOUR-WITH-INTACT-MEMBRANES-2.0.pdf)

At the limits of viability [when survival outside the womb becomes possible], ask the obstetrician and neonatologist for the receiving unit's current policy and outcomes rather than using overseas survival figures as a local promise. [SA national guideline](https://knowledgehub.health.gov.za/system/files/elibdownloads/2024-10/Integrated%20Maternal%20and%20Perinatal%20Care%20Guideline_Final%204%20October%202024%20%20DG%20signed.pdf)

NICE permits consideration of emergency cerclage through 27 weeks and 6 days in selected cases with unruptured membranes, so 24 weeks is not a universal cutoff for every type of stitch. [NICE emergency-cerclage recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng25/chapter/recommendations)

Grief and pregnancy planning can move at different speeds for each partner, and counselling can support both without requiring a shared timetable. [Tommy's pregnancy-after-loss information](https://www.tommys.org/baby-loss-support/stillbirth-information-and-support/trying-another-baby-after-stillbirth-neonatal-death)

The Highlands North organisation has a primary-source pregnancy-loss group listing from August 2026, but its next date still needs confirmation. [The Compassionate Friends](https://www.compassionatefriends.co.za/supportgroups/general-grief-support-group-14-june-kdwp7-z8czs-wjn7g)
